beginner: Marigolds are easy, cheerful flowers and the classic companion plant, grown for blooms rather than food. They love heat and full sun, handle poor soil and dry spells, and bloom from summer until the first fall frost. There are three main kinds: small bushy French marigolds, tall big-flowered African (or American) marigolds, and tiny lacy Signet marigolds with edible petals. Plant the seeds outside after your last frost once the soil is warm, and you get flowers in about two months. Keep snipping off faded blooms to get more. Their most proven garden trick is fighting soil nematodes: grow a thick patch of French marigolds and dig them in before planting vegetables that nematodes attack.
seasoned: Marigold (Tagetes species) is a warm-season, frost-tender annual in the Asteraceae family, native to Mexico and Central America. It is grown for showy blooms and as the classic companion plant, in three main types: compact French marigolds (Tagetes patula), tall large-pompon African or American marigolds (Tagetes erecta), and petite, lacy, edible-flowered Signet marigolds (Tagetes tenuifolia). Sown into warm soil after frost, it reaches first bloom in roughly 7 to 9 weeks and flowers continuously from summer until the first fall frost. It thrives in heat, full sun, and even poor soil, and is notably drought-tolerant once established. Its best-supported pest function is nematode suppression: French marigolds grown as a dense cover stand and incorporated lower root-knot nematode populations for the following crop.

beginner: Marigolds are not fussy and grow in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. Soil that is moderately fertile and well drained is ideal; very rich soil grows lots of leaves and fewer flowers. Avoid soggy ground, which rots the roots. If your soil is very acidic, the leaves can speckle bronze, so a normal garden range works best.
seasoned: Marigolds want moderately fertile, well-drained soil and tolerate a wide range of textures, including poorer ground; the consistent failure is wet, poorly drained soil that rots roots and crowns. They are light feeders, so over-rich soil pushes foliage at the expense of bloom. On strongly acidic soil (below about pH 5.5), foliage can show a bronze speckling from manganese or iron toxicity, so a near-neutral range is preferred.

beginner: Marigolds are not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range around 6.0 to 7.0 is ideal, and you usually do not need to change anything. Only very acidic soil, below about 5.5, can cause speckled, bronze-looking leaves.
seasoned: Marigolds perform best across roughly 6.0 to 7.0 and tolerate a little outside that. No pH adjustment is typically warranted, but strongly acidic soil (below about 5.5) can trigger manganese or iron toxicity that bronze-speckles the foliage, so favor a near-neutral bed.

beginner: Wait until the soil is warm (about 65 to 70 °F) before planting marigold seeds outside; they sprout in under a week in warm soil. Go easy on fertilizer and do not overwater, since both give you lots of leaves but fewer flowers. Snip off faded blooms (deadheading) to keep more coming. If you have a nematode problem in a vegetable bed, the trick that actually works is to plant a thick patch of French marigolds there for a couple of months first, then dig them in, not just dotting a few among your vegetables.
seasoned: Soil warmth, not the calendar, is the real germination trigger: direct-sow into soil near 65 to 70 °F after frost and seedlings break ground in 5 to 8 days. Go light on nitrogen and avoid overwatering, both of which give leaves at the expense of bloom; deadhead or cut for the vase to sustain flowering to frost. For root-knot nematode pressure, grow French types (Tagetes patula) as a dense, solid cover stand for two months before the susceptible crop, then turn them under, rather than scattering a few among the vegetables.

beginner: Marigolds do not need much feeding. Mix a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the soil before planting and that is usually plenty. Too much fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind, gives you leaves instead of flowers, so go light.
seasoned: Marigolds are light feeders; a modest balanced dose worked into the soil at planting is usually all they need. Excess nitrogen pushes soft, leafy growth and suppresses bloom, so favor a balanced or slightly lower-nitrogen feed over a high-nitrogen one, and skip routine feeding once established.

beginner: It is a good time to give your marigolds a little feed if you want. They do not need much, so one light dose of a balanced fertilizer is plenty, and you can skip it if you already worked some into the soil at planting.
seasoned: Time for an optional light feed. Marigolds are light feeders, so one modest dose of a balanced fertilizer supports steady bloom; skip it entirely if you mixed compost or fertilizer into the bed at planting.

beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For marigolds, pick a balanced one like 10-10-10 rather than a high first-number (nitrogen) lawn feed, which gives leaves instead of flowers.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting suits marigolds better than a high-nitrogen lawn-type feed, which favors foliage over flowers.

beginner: A little goes a long way. One light feeding when you plant is usually enough. If you do feed again, use about half the amount the package suggests, and avoid high-nitrogen feeds.
seasoned: A single light application at planting is usually sufficient; if supplementing, use a balanced fertilizer at about half the label rate for annual flowers. Avoid repeated high-nitrogen feeding, which favors foliage over bloom.

beginner: Keep the soil damp while seeds sprout and plants get going. After that, water deeply but less often. Grown marigolds handle dry spells well, so you do not need to water every day, and soggy soil does more harm than dryness.
seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and establishment, then water deeply but less often; established marigolds are notably drought-tolerant, and over-frequent shallow watering invites root rot and foliar disease.

beginner: Marigolds like about one inch of water a week, counting rain. Water deeply once or twice a week instead of a little every day, and let the soil dry out a bit between waterings. Once established, they handle dry spells well.
seasoned: Aim for roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, applied deeply and less often rather than in frequent shallow doses; let the soil dry somewhat between waterings. Established and especially African and Signet plantings tolerate less.

beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves. A soaker hose or watering can at the base works best. Tall marigolds especially can flop or rot if you spray water over the top, so keep the flowers dry; if leaves get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday.
seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and avoid overhead wetting; on the tall African types in particular, overhead watering breaks stems and leaves the dense blooms wet, which invites gray mold. If you must use a sprinkler, water in the morning so foliage dries fast.

beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base looks soft and mushy, you are likely overwatering or the soil drains poorly. Wet flowers also turn moldy.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, rotting stems or crowns signal overwatering or poor drainage; persistently wet, dense blooms also raise gray-mold pressure. Dwarf French types rot readily if kept saturated.

beginner: Marigolds that are too dry wilt in the afternoon heat, look dull, and make smaller flowers. They are thirstiest right after planting and when the first buds form, but established plants bounce back from short dry spells.
seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day that recovers by evening, dulling leaf color, and reduced flower size at bud point indicate underwatering, most critically during establishment and at first bloom; established plants are forgiving of short dry spells.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp until the seedlings come up. This is when marigolds most need steady water.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed evenly moist through germination and establishment, marigold's one critical moisture window.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered while they get going.
seasoned: Grow seedlings on with steady moisture while they establish; after that, water deeply but less often.

beginner: Established marigolds handle dry spells well. About an inch a week, deep and less often, letting the soil dry a bit between waterings. Frequent shallow watering causes rot, and the little French types especially rot in soggy soil.
seasoned: Established marigolds are notably drought-tolerant: about an inch a week applied deeply and less often, letting the soil dry somewhat between waterings. Over-frequent shallow watering invites root rot and foliar disease, and dwarf French types rot readily if kept saturated.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist as the first buds form. Letting marigolds get too dry right at budding gives smaller, fewer flowers.
seasoned: Keep even moisture as the first buds form: drought stress at first bud reduces flower size and count, so do not let a budding plant bake dry even though it is drought-adapted.

beginner: While marigolds bloom, water at the base and keep the flower heads dry. On the tall types, watering from above snaps the stems and the wet heads get gray mold.
seasoned: Through bloom, water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and keep water off the dense heads: on tall African types especially, overhead watering breaks stems and leaves the blooms wet, which invites gray mold.

beginner: As the flower heads dry for seed, they need little or no water.
seasoned: As the heads dry to save seed, little to no water is needed; a dry finish ripens the seed for collecting.

beginner: Water the soil around the plant, not the leaves or flowers. A soaker hose or a watering can at the base works best, because dry, airy plants resist mold. Avoid spraying water over the top of tall marigolds, which can break their stems.
seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and keep water off the foliage and blooms; dry, well-spaced plants are the main cultural lever against gray mold and leaf spot. Avoid overhead sprinkling on tall African types, whose heavy wet heads snap stems.

beginner: Marigolds are flowers for the garden and the vase, not food to store, so there is nothing to refrigerate or freeze. To make cut flowers last, trim the stems, pull off the smelly lower leaves that would sit underwater, and use a clean vase with fresh water. They usually stay nice for several days to a week. The small Signet marigolds have edible petals with a spicy, tarragon-like flavor, used fresh.
seasoned: Marigold is grown for bloom and companion value, not as a stored edible, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply. For cut flowers, recut stems and strip the strongly scented lower leaves below the waterline (they foul vase water fast), use clean water with floral preservative, and keep blooms out of direct sun. Vase life is several days to about a week. The Signet types have edible, spicy-tarragon petals used fresh as a garnish.

beginner: Pick the type for your spot. French marigolds are small, bushy, and bloom for a long time, perfect for beds, pots, and edging, and they are the type that suppresses soil nematodes when planted thickly. African marigolds are the tall ones with big round pompon flowers, good at the back of a bed and for cutting. Signet marigolds are tiny, lacy plants covered in small flowers, very tough in heat and drought, with petals you can eat. Open, single flowers are best for bees and butterflies.
seasoned: Choose by type and purpose. French marigolds (Tagetes patula) are the compact, bushy, long-blooming bedding and edging workhorses and the type to use for root-knot nematode cover plantings (cultivars such as 'Single Gold' and 'Tangerine' are the trialed performers). African or American marigolds (Tagetes erecta) are the tall, large-pompon types for the back of the border and for cutting; they benefit most from deadheading and staking. Signet marigolds (Tagetes tenuifolia) are the petite, lacy, heat- and drought-tough edgers, smothered in small single flowers whose petals are edible. Single, open-faced flowers serve pollinators better than the densest doubles.

beginner: Marigolds are the classic companion plant, grown to help the rest of the garden more than for themselves. The one pest benefit that research actually supports is against root-knot nematodes (tiny soil worms that damage roots): if you grow a thick, solid patch of French marigolds in a problem bed for about two months and then dig them in, before planting a crop that nematodes attack, they can lower the nematode numbers. Just dotting a few marigolds among your vegetables has not been shown to do this. The old idea that their strong smell drives away insects, rabbits, and deer is traditional belief, sometimes helpful but not reliable. What marigolds clearly do is bring in bees and helpful insects, so they are a cheerful, useful edge or border plant almost anywhere. There is no plant you must keep them away from; just give them room and sun.
seasoned: Marigold inverts the usual companion framing: it is the plant you place to benefit others. Its one research-supported pest function is nematode suppression, and only in a specific form: French marigolds (Tagetes patula) grown as a dense, weed-free solid stand for about two months in the target bed and then incorporated, ahead of a susceptible crop, can reduce root-knot and lesion nematode populations via root-released alpha-terthienyl. UF/IFAS is explicit that simply interplanting a few marigolds among vegetables has not been shown to reduce nematodes, and the African types are less effective than French for this. The broader reputation, that marigold scent repels insects, rabbits, and deer, is traditional companion lore: sometimes borne out, not reliably documented. What is solid is that marigold is a strong pollinator and beneficial-insect draw, so it earns its place as an insectary edge or border. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; site for sun and airflow.

beginner: If a bed has root-knot nematodes, grow a thick patch of French marigolds there for about two months, then dig them in, before planting vegetables that nematodes attack. This is the marigold trick that research actually backs.
seasoned: This is marigold's evidence-based pest function. French marigolds planted as a dense, weed-free solid stand for about two months and then incorporated, ahead of the susceptible crop, reduce root-knot and lesion nematode populations through root-released alpha-terthienyl. It is a sequential, whole-bed treatment, not a concurrent interplant: keep the stand free of grass and weeds (so nematodes cannot feed on other roots) and follow with the vegetable crop the next season. African types are less effective than French.

beginner: Marigolds are traditionally planted with tomatoes and peppers, and they do draw in bees and helpful predator insects. The idea that their smell repels pests is folklore, so enjoy the flowers and beneficial bugs and do not count on them as bug spray.
seasoned: A traditional pairing whose real, defensible benefit is beneficial-insect habitat rather than pest repellence. Marigold nectar and pollen draw hoverflies, lacewings, ladybugs, and parasitic wasps whose larvae prey on aphids and other soft-bodied pests of tomatoes and peppers. Note the honest limits: the popular claims that marigold scent repels pests, and that interplanting a few marigolds controls the nematodes that bother tomatoes, are not supported by extension trials. Plant them as an insectary edge for predator support and color, not as a substitute for pest control.

beginner: Squash, melons, and cucumbers need insects to move pollen to set fruit. Marigolds bloom a long time and bring in the bees that do that job.
seasoned: A well-grounded pollinator pairing. Cucurbits depend on insect pollination, with several bee visits needed per flower for proper fruit set, and marigold is a reliable, long-blooming pollinator magnet across the cucurbit fruiting window. More pollinator traffic plausibly means better set and fewer aborted fruits. Plant marigolds in nearby rows so the pollinators they draw spill onto the crop; this is a visitation benefit, not a pest-control one.

beginner: Marigolds add color and bring in helpful bugs alongside cabbage-family crops and beans without crowding them for food. Traditionally they are also planted to deter pests, though that part is folklore.
seasoned: A habitat-level pairing. Marigold adds beneficial-insect and pollinator habitat alongside cabbage-family crops and beans with low nutrient competition, and the flowers support parasitic wasps and predators that help manage aphids and caterpillars. The traditional claim that marigold scent deters cabbage pests and bean beetles is not extension-verified; treat it as a loose, garden-ecosystem pairing, kept to the edges so it does not shade lower crops.

beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they get used to sun and wind before you plant them out.
seasoned: Indoor-started transplants need 7 to 10 days of hardening off, increasing outdoor exposure gradually, before transplanting after all frost danger has passed.

beginner: The easiest way is to sow marigold seeds straight into warm garden soil (about 65 to 70 °F) after your last frost, a quarter inch deep; they sprout in under a week. For a head start, or for the tall African types, start them indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost (about 8 weeks for African) and move them outside afterward. You can pinch the tops of tall types once to make them bushier.
seasoned: Marigolds direct-sow readily into warm soil (about 65 to 70 °F) at 1/4 in depth and germinate in 5 to 8 days, the simplest method in long-season areas. To gain weeks or for the slow-developing tall African types, start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost (up to 8 weeks for African) and transplant after frost. Pinch tall African types once to encourage branching; French and Signet types need no pinching.

beginner: Marigolds are in the daisy family (Asteraceae). If they had a lot of disease, do not plant them, or other daisy-family flowers, in the same spot the very next season. On the flip side, a thick planting of French marigolds is actually a good thing to grow before nematode-prone vegetables, because it lowers the nematodes in that soil.
seasoned: As an aster-family (Asteraceae) annual, avoid following marigold immediately with other susceptible asters where soilborne or foliar disease has built up; rotate the bed to an unrelated family for a season if gray mold or leaf spot was heavy. Note the inverse: a French marigold stand is itself a beneficial rotation tool, lowering root-knot nematode pressure for the crop that follows.

beginner: Rotating marigolds is not as important as it is for vegetables, but it still helps. Plant them in a different spot each year if you can, and clean up old, diseased leaves at the end of the season. Used on purpose, a thick patch of French marigolds grown for a couple of months and then dug in is a real way to cut down soil nematodes before you plant vegetables there.
seasoned: Rotation matters less for a fast-growing ornamental annual than for heavy-feeding vegetables, but moving marigolds to a fresh bed each year and clearing infected debris at season end limits carryover of gray-mold and leaf-spot inoculum. Used deliberately, a two-month French marigold cover stand turned under is a documented preceding-crop treatment for root-knot nematodes.

beginner: Plant seeds outside only once the soil is warm, around 65 to 70 °F. Cold, wet soil makes seeds rot instead of sprout. In warm soil they come up in under a week.
seasoned: Direct-sow once soil is near 65 to 70 °F; warmth, not the calendar date, is the germination trigger, and seed sown into cold, wet soil rots or damps off. In warm soil, marigolds sprout in 5 to 8 days.

beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter inch deep. In warm soil they sprout fast, so planting straight in the ground works well.
seasoned: Sow at about 1/4 in depth; marigolds germinate quickly and reliably in warm soil, which makes direct sowing the simplest method in long-season areas.

beginner: Once seedlings have a few real leaves, space them out: small types about 8 to 10 inches apart, tall types about a foot. Room for air to move helps prevent mold.
seasoned: Thin or space seedlings by type once they have a few true leaves: French and Signet to 8 to 10 in, tall African to 12 to 16 in. Generous spacing for airflow is a primary cultural defense against gray mold and leaf spot.

beginner: Keep an eye on young marigolds for slugs and snails, which chew tender seedlings in damp weather. Hand-pick them at night or use a pet-safe iron-phosphate bait.
seasoned: Watch young marigolds for slugs and snails in damp weather; seedlings are a frequent target. Reduce mulch harborage, hand-pick at night, or use iron-phosphate bait, and water at the base.

beginner: If you are growing tall marigolds, pinch off the top once to make them bushier with more flowers. Small types do this by themselves. Go easy on fertilizer so you get flowers, not just leaves.
seasoned: Pinch the growing tip of tall African types once to force branching and more, sturdier stems; French and Signet types branch naturally and need no pinching. Keep nitrogen modest so plants flower rather than run to foliage.

beginner: As plants grow, keep air moving between them and water the soil, not the leaves. Full sun, space, and dry leaves are what keep mold away, especially in humid areas.
seasoned: Maintain airflow and water at the base as plants fill in; full sun, spacing, and dry foliage keep gray mold and leaf spot in check, sharpest where humidity is high.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist when the first flower buds appear, but not soggy. Too dry means smaller flowers; too wet rots the plant.
seasoned: Keep moisture even as the first buds form; drought stress at bud point reduces flower size and count, but never let the soil stay wet, which rots roots and buds.

beginner: As buds form, check for tiny spider mites in hot, dry weather and for gray mold on the buds in damp weather. Catching crowding and watering problems early keeps both down.
seasoned: Scout for spider mites in hot, dry spells (marigold's most characteristic pest) and for gray mold on dense buds in damp weather; addressing crowding and dryness early limits both.

beginner: Snip off faded flowers back to the next set of leaves (or cut fresh ones for a vase) to get more blooms until the first fall frost. The small French types keep blooming on their own, but the big types flower more if you deadhead.
seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms back to the next leaf node, or cut for the vase, to redirect energy from seed set into new flowers and sustain bloom to first frost. French types rebloom well even without deadheading; African types benefit most from it.

beginner: If you want marigolds to fight soil nematodes, the method that works is to grow a thick patch of French marigolds in the problem bed for about two months, then dig them in, before planting vegetables there. Just scattering a few among your crops does not do it.
seasoned: For a documented nematode benefit, treat French marigolds as a cover crop, not a casual interplant: grow a dense, weed-free solid stand for about two months in the target bed, then incorporate it, ahead of the susceptible crop. Interplanting a few among vegetables has not been shown to reduce nematodes.

beginner: To save seeds, leave a few flowers on the plant and let them dry and turn brown before picking them. Note that seeds from hybrid marigolds will not grow into the same flower next year.
seasoned: To save seed, leave some heads on the plant to dry fully to brown before collecting; most modern bedding marigolds are hybrids, so their seed will not come true to type.

beginner: One marigold gives you lots of flowers over the summer. The small French and Signet types make many small blooms at once, while the tall African types make fewer but big, showy flowers good for cutting. Keep picking faded flowers and they keep coming until frost.
seasoned: A single marigold blooms profusely over a season; French and Signet types carry dozens of small to medium flowers continuously, while the tall African types produce fewer but much larger pompon blooms well suited to cutting. Deadheading or cutting sustains production to frost.

beginner: Marigolds flower the same year you plant them, usually about two months after sowing. There is no waiting year. Plant in spring and you will have flowers from summer until the first frost.
seasoned: Marigolds bloom the first season from seed, roughly 7 to 9 weeks after sowing (French sooner, African later), so there is no establishment year; a spring sowing flowers from early summer to first frost.

beginner: Flowers turned mushy with gray fuzz

seasoned: Botrytis gray mold took hold, favored by humidity, crowding, and overhead wetness; the dense double African blooms rot from the center.

beginner: Give plants more room next time, water the soil instead of the flowers, plant in full sun, and pick off faded blooms before they rot.

beginner: Deadheading means snipping off flowers once they fade. Do it regularly: cut the old bloom back to the next set of leaves, and the plant makes more flowers instead of going to seed.
